skills.title: Read a map using its three components: distance (scale), direction and symbols
Tell latitudes (parallels) from longitudes (meridians) and name the key lines: Equator, Tropics, Prime Meridian
Locate a place from its latitude and longitude on a globe or map
Explain the Ujjain meridian and Greenwich Prime Meridian as reference lines, and use 15° = 1 hour to reason about time zones and IST

expectations: A map shows places using a scale (map distance stands for real distance), directions (north, south, east, west and in-between) and symbols (signs and colours with a key).
Latitudes (parallels) are imaginary circles running east-west; they tell how far north or south of the Equator (0°) a place is, up to 90° at each pole.
Longitudes (meridians) are imaginary half-circles running from pole to pole; they tell how far east or west of the Prime Meridian (0°, Greenwich) a place is, up to 180°.
A place is located exactly where its latitude line and longitude line cross, for example New Delhi is about 28.6°N, 77.2°E.
Long before Greenwich was chosen, Indian astronomers used a reference meridian (madhya rekha) passing through Ujjain for their calculations.
The Earth turns 360° in about 24 hours, so 15° of longitude makes 1 hour of time difference; Indian Standard Time is based on 82.5°E and is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich time.

expectations: About 71% of the Earth's surface is water and about 29% is land, which is why it is called the 'blue planet'.
There are seven continents: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia; Asia is the largest and Australia the smallest.
There are five oceans: Pacific (largest and deepest), Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic (smallest); they are all connected.
India is a country in the continent of Asia, with the Indian Ocean to its south, the Arabian Sea to the west and the Bay of Bengal to the east.
Oceans give food and salt, affect weather and rainfall (including the monsoon), and have been highways for trade, such as old sea routes from India's coast to Africa, Arabia and South-East Asia.

skills.title: Describe different kinds of families (joint, nuclear and others) and how members care for and support one another
Explain how responsibilities at home can be shared fairly, including children's roles
Describe how communities support their members through shared work, festivals, community kitchens and help in hard times
Connect family and community values to the wider society (interdependence, 'the world is one family')

expectations: Families come in many forms: joint families (grandparents, parents, uncles, aunts, cousins together), nuclear families (parents and children) and others; all can be caring families.
In a family, members support each other: care for children and elders, share work and money, and pass on values, skills, stories and traditions.
Responsibilities work best when shared fairly by everyone according to their ability, including children doing age-appropriate tasks.

A community is a larger group of people who live or work together and help one another, for example neighbours, a village or a housing colony; community kitchens like the langar at gurdwaras serve everyone freely.
Families and communities depend on each other; the old idea 'vasudhaiva kutumbakam' (the world is one family) extends this care to all people.

expectations: Governance is the way a society is run: making rules, carrying them out, providing services such as roads, water and schools, and settling disputes; a government is the body that does this.

expectations: Panchayati Raj is the system of local self-government in villages, with three tiers: gram panchayat (village), panchayat samiti (block) and zila parishad (district); it was given constitutional status by the 73rd Amendment (1992).

The gram sabha is the meeting of all adults (18 years and above) whose names are on the voters' list of the panchayat area; it discusses plans, checks the panchayat's work and helps choose who benefits from schemes.
The gram panchayat is made of elected ward members (panch) and a head (sarpanch, also called pradhan or mukhiya), elected every five years; a secretary appointed by the government keeps records.

The panchayat looks after local needs such as drinking water, village roads, drains, street lights, cleanliness and carrying out government schemes; it gets money from local taxes and government grants.
At least one-third of seats are reserved for women (many states reserve half), and seats are also reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, so that all groups have a voice.

expectations: Towns and cities have urban local bodies: municipal corporations for large cities, municipal councils for smaller cities and towns, and nagar panchayats for areas changing from rural to urban; they got constitutional status through the 74th Amendment (1992).

skills.title: Classify an activity as primary (from nature), secondary (making goods) or tertiary (services)
Trace a product's chain from nature to the customer through the three sectors
Explain how the sectors depend on each other (cause-effect)

expectations: Primary activities take things directly from nature: farming, fishing, animal rearing, forestry and mining.
Secondary activities turn raw materials into finished goods: textile mills, sugar mills, bakeries, furniture making and construction.
Tertiary activities provide services that support the others and people: transport, shops and trade, banking, teaching, health care and communication.
Products often pass through all three: cotton grown on a farm (primary) is spun and woven into cloth in a mill (secondary) and transported and sold in a shop (tertiary).
The sectors depend on each other: if one stops, the others are affected, and different regions specialise based on their resources.
